references.text: Direct continuation specifying that the water rose 15 cubits above the mountains that were covered.
Describes how the floodwaters gradually receded and the mountain peaks became visible again, which is a direct contrast to the water covering all the mountains.
The poetry reflects on how God covered the earth with water like a garment, and how the mountains rose and the valleys sank – a poetic description that mirrors the power of the waters in the flood.
Peter explicitly refers to the ancient world being flooded by water and perishing, a direct reference to the universal flood where the water covered the whole earth.
Refers to God's power to send water that floods the earth, relevant to the theme of the overwhelming power of water.
Psalm 104:6 alludes directly to the height of the flood above the mountains to illustrate God's sovereignty over creation.
Creates a theological contrast between the order of creation (the earth above the water) and the chaos of the flood (the water above the earth).
Direct narrative connection; the verses describe respectively the beginning and the peak of the same flood event.
2 Peter 3:6 alludes directly to the flood in Genesis as an example of God's judgment on the world.
